blurb: Dr. K hosts the finale: the study itself — four research questions, four design requirements, a 300-paragraph human reference set, and nested tests that hold the adjudicator constant. No new scores here: learn to explain the method, not just quote the results.
intro: Dr. K here, and this last episode is about the study itself — not the scores, but how they were earned. If you can explain the method, you can defend the result. And if you can't, the result isn't worth much. Four questions, four requirements, one human reference set, and a nested test that keeps the adjudicator honest.

body: ADAM began as four research questions — and four design requirements built to answer them. The alignment is deliberate: each question has a requirement that forces the design to take it seriously.

RQ1 — How can a DSS coordinate lexicon, transformer, and contextual-quality evidence? RQ2 — Does agentic adjudication improve interpretation, and is the gain architectural? RQ3 — What explains disagreement, and does it identify passages needing review? RQ4 — Are confidence-aware outputs useful for prioritization and economically relevant?

The four design requirements: DR1 — Preserve heterogeneous evidence. DR2 — Diagnose disagreement. DR3 — Qualify signals with temporal / disclosure context. DR4 — Maintain traceability to source text. RQ1 is the design question; RQ2 asks whether the architecture adds value beyond its components; RQ3 treats disagreement as a diagnostic phenomenon; RQ4 moves from predictive accuracy to decision-support behaviour and economic relevance.
lessons.tip: A design-science study is judged by its questions and its requirements, not only by its accuracy table. Keep RQ2 in mind all episode — it is the question the whole evaluation is built to answer.

body: The empirical setting: 55 firms, five from each of 11 GICS sectors, over 2016–2025 — 550 firm-year 10-Ks. The focal paragraphs come from Item 1A and Item 7: 179,623 in total (94,031 Item 1A + 85,592 Item 7). Filings from 2014–2015 (32,407 paragraphs) are used only as historical context, to initialize the longitudinal measures — so the system can tell what is new from what is carried over. (Slide 10 also prints “143,372 focal paragraphs”; the Item counts sum to 179,623, the figure used here and in Episode 1.)

The primary unit is the paragraph — the contextualized paragraph object, linked to firm, year, section, sector, prior-year context, peer context, and provenance. ADAM focuses on Item 1A and Item 7 because they are narrative-heavy but have different linguistic baselines.

The evaluation rests on a human reference set: 300 paragraphs (144 Item 1A, 156 Item 7, 2016–2025, all 11 sectors), each independently reviewed by 3 reviewers who were blinded to all LM, FinBERT, and ADAM outputs. Review packets included the target paragraph, surrounding text when available, and relevant prior-year context — but no model outputs. Each reviewer annotated four constructs: linguistic sentiment, economic direction, disclosure informativeness, and interpretive ambiguity.

The headline finding about the humans: unanimous agreement was only 21% for sentiment, 25% for economic direction, and 32% for informativeness. Most of the rest had a two-of-three majority. Interpretive disagreement is not only annotation noise — it becomes an empirical signal of task difficulty. Chance-corrected reliability statistics are to be reported in the final manuscript.
lessons.h: The data and the human reference set
lessons.tip: If three careful humans agree unanimously only one time in five, a model that claims 99% certainty on this task is not confident — it is overconfident. That is why ADAM routes its uncertainty to review instead of hiding it.

body: The evaluation separates two questions: how good is ADAM versus established methods — and does any gain come from the architecture rather than from putting an LLM at the end? The nested tests hold the adjudicator constant and progressively add structured evidence: LM dictionary (lexical baseline); FinBERT (contextual baseline); LM + FinBERT simple non-agentic ensemble; Judge-only (same adjudicator, paragraph only); Base evidence (paragraph + LM + FinBERT); Full ADAM (+ Context & Quality evidence).

What is evaluated: accuracy + macro-F1, class-level precision / recall, agreement vs disagreement cases, adjudicator resolution behaviour, human-disagreement / review-needed alignment, and external financial validation. The nested design is the point: Judge-only tells you what the LLM can do by itself, so any gain from Base or Full ADAM has to come from the evidence and the architecture — not from a better LLM.

The contributions come in three buckets. DSS design: a modular architecture for coordinating heterogeneous analytical evidence while preserving traceability and uncertainty. Conceptual: treat model disagreement as potentially diagnostic evidence — not merely noise or a failure to be averaged away. Evaluation: combine human reference labels, conventional benchmarks, nested ablations, disagreement analysis, and external validation.

The logic generalizes beyond SEC filings: the same evidence-coordination logic can apply whenever multiple analytical methods read complex narratives differently — regulatory, legal, clinical, cybersecurity, or operational text. The design-science framing follows Hevner et al. (2004), with Gregor & Hevner (2013). Next steps: finalize the Context & Quality Agent operationalization, confirmatory validation, disagreement analysis, and architecture ablations.

game.done: Six arms, one adjudicator held constant — that is how you separate the architecture's work from the LLM's work.
game.hint: Not quite — ask what evidence the adjudicator was given: paragraph only, paragraph + two agents, or everything?
game.intro: Six evaluation arms, one adjudicator held constant. Sort each setup into the arm it belongs to.

items.t: The adjudicator reads the paragraph alone — no LM scores, no FinBERT probabilities, no context.
items.why: Paragraph only, same adjudicator. This is the “what can the LLM do by itself?” arm.

items.t: Paragraph + LM + FinBERT evidence, but nothing about novelty, persistence, or peers.
items.why: Base evidence adds the two sentiment agents but not the Context & Quality Agent.

items.t: Paragraph + LM + FinBERT + Context & Quality evidence — the complete system.
items.why: Full ADAM is the complete architecture; the jump from Base to Full is the architecture test.

items.t: Same adjudicator, same paragraph — but the paragraph is the only thing in the room.
items.why: Still paragraph only. If this arm already scores 82% on sentiment, the LLM is doing most of that work.

game.title: Dr. K Challenge: Which evaluation arm is this?

lessons.h: The evaluation design — and what the study contributes
lessons.tip: Judge-only is the most honest control in the whole study. Without it, every gain could be credited to the architecture when it really belongs to the LLM.

outro: That's the whole quest — and the three takeaways to carry out the door: (1) Different models see different evidence — do not collapse that evidence too early. (2) Disagreement can be diagnostically useful — ask why methods diverge, and whether the conflict is resolvable. (3) Decision support is more than accuracy — traceability, uncertainty, context, and human attention are part of the output. You can now explain the study, not just quote its scores. Go read a disclosure like an adjudicator.

opts: To separate whether the architecture adds value from whether the LLM alone does the work
To test six different LLMs against each other
To make the accuracy numbers higher
quiz.q: Why does ADAM's evaluation use nested tests that hold the adjudicator constant?
quiz.why: Holding the adjudicator constant while progressively adding evidence separates whether the architecture adds value from whether the LLM alone does the work. Judge-only shows what the LLM does by itself (82.0% sentiment, 84.0% direction); only gains above that can be credited to the evidence and the architecture. Testing different LLMs or comparing sections is not what the nested design does.

quiz.q: Which evaluation arm gives the adjudicator the paragraph plus LM and FinBERT evidence, but NO Context & Quality evidence?
quiz.why: Base evidence is paragraph + LM + FinBERT. Judge-only is the paragraph alone; Full ADAM adds the Context & Quality evidence; the LM + FinBERT ensemble is a simple non-agentic combination with no adjudicator at all.

opts: The task is genuinely difficult, and interpretive disagreement is a signal of task difficulty, not only annotation noise
The reviewers were not blinded properly
Sentiment labels should be dropped from ADAM
The 300-paragraph set is too small to use
quiz.q: Reviewers agreed unanimously on only 21% of paragraphs for sentiment. What does the study conclude from this?
quiz.why: Unanimous agreement was only 21% for sentiment, 25% for direction, and 32% for informativeness — and the study treats that as evidence the task is genuinely interpretive, with disagreement as a signal of difficulty rather than only annotation noise. The reviewers were blinded to all model outputs, and chance-corrected reliability statistics are to be reported in the final manuscript.
